The winners of the 2026 Tonnellerie de Mercurey Young Winemaker of the Year and the 2026 Young Viticulturist of the Year competitions have been revealed following a celebration dinner at Tākina Wellington Convention and Exhibition Centre last night.

30-year-old Nick Lamain from Isabel Estate in Marlborough is the 2026 Young Winemaker of the Year, and 24-year-old Kris Godsall from Cloudy Bay is the 2026 Young Viticulturist of the Year.

“Honestly, it still feels a little surreal. I’ve been part of this competition for the past five years, and it has challenged me, built my confidence, and played a huge role in shaping my career. To cap off that journey by taking out the national title is an incredible honour, and a moment I’ll be proud of for a very long time,” said Lamain.

“It’s a lot to take in,” said Kris Godsall.

“It’s a prestigious title to win, and all the hard work has paid off.”

The Young Winemaker national finals were held on 25 August at The Runholder, and the Young Viticulturist national finals were held at Escarpment the following day.

New Zealand Winegrowers extended congratulations to Heath Miller from Pask in Hawke’s Bay, who came second in the Young Viticulturist competition, and Joshua Irving from Lincoln University in North Canterbury, who placed third.

The other Young Viticulturists competing were Alex Coombs from Craggy Range in Wairarapa and Braxton Benseman from Mt. Difficulty in Central Otago. The other Young Winemakers were Aaron Coxhead from Coxhead Wines in Waikato/Bay of Plenty and Joshua Irving from Lincoln University in North Canterbury.

For the Young Winemakers, the challenges included the Constellation Brands Laboratory Section and the Indevin Wine Judging section, both won by Lamain. They also gave a presentation on how the wine industry could continue to reduce its carbon footprint. They finished by delivering their Fruitfed Supplies speeches at the New Zealand Wine 2026 Wine Business Forum at Te Papa on Thursday afternoon. Their topic was about wine tourism opportunities in their regions. This was won by Joshua Irving.

The challenges for the Young Viticulturists included machinery, an interview, a mock vineyard tour and a leadership challenge. They also had to write a report and give a presentation on cost savings in the vineyard and preparing for a potential super El Niño. They went head-to-head in the Ecotrellis trellising section, which was won by Heath Miller, as well as the BioStart Hortisports, taken out by Kris Godsall. They finished by delivering their speeches to a large industry crowd at the New Zealand Wine 2026 Celebration Dinner.

Godsall won a prize package including a $6,000 Ecotrellis Travel Grant, a leadership week, a piece of artwork and cash.

Lamain won a trip to Burgundy to visit the Tonnellerie de Mercurey (cooperage), a piece of artwork, the opportunity to be an associate judge at the New World Wine Awards and to review wines for Drinks Biz Magazine.

Both national winners will be heading to Sauvignon Blanc New Zealand 2027 in February and the Organic Winegrowers Conference next June.

Fruitfed Supplies is providing a field trip for all the Young Viticulturist and Winemaker national finalists so that they can “continue to upskill and reconnect post-competition”.

content:
Thousands of tonnes of Marlborough winery waste could be transformed into a valuable resource for vineyards through a new regional programme led by Bragato Research Institute (BRI).

The Marlborough Circular Wine Programme will collect winery lees, the sediment left over from winemaking, and combine it with materials such as compost and biochar to produce a safe, beneficial soil amendment. The initiative aims to reduce waste and emissions while returning organic matter and nutrients to vineyard soils.

BRI explained that large volumes of lees are produced over a relatively short winemaking period during and after vintage.

“They can be expensive to dispose of and place pressure on regional wastewater and waste-management infrastructure. As disposal costs rise and environmental expectations increase, Marlborough wineries need a more sustainable regional alternative,” the organisation said.

Programme leader Dr Seth Laurenson said that the goal is to create a coordinated regional system that safely returns organic matter and its nutrients to vineyard soils.

“This programme is an excellent example of the wine industry, researchers and government working together to solve a costly waste problem and turn it into a regional resource,” said Dr Laurenson.

The programme will “collect lees from participating wineries and process them into a beneficial soil amendment”. Wineries pay a disposal fee “designed to be competitive with landfill costs” and the finished product will be returned to participating vineyards at no additional cost.

Over four years, the programme aims to divert more than 3,500 tonnes of solid lees from landfill and wastewater systems each year, “mitigating around 4,700 tonnes of CO₂-equivalent emissions”.

The four-year programme represents a combined investment of $6.98 million. The government is investing $2.79 million through the Primary Sector Growth Fund, alongside $4.19 million in co-investment from New Zealand Winegrowers and participating wineries. The programme is also supported by The Green Circle and Marlborough District Council.

BRI will lead the scientific testing, quality assurance and system design needed to demonstrate that the model is sustainable and practical at commercial scale. The programme will also develop a business case for establishing a permanent regional facility.

The Marlborough Circular Wine Programme is the first initiative of its kind at commercial scale in New Zealand’s wine sector.

“If we can demonstrate a safe and commercially viable model in Marlborough, the approach could provide a blueprint for other wine regions,” said Dr Laurenson.

The Adelaide Hills Cup was hosted Saturday 22 August at Simon Tolley Wines. Image supplied

On Saturday 22 August, Stefan Sancin took out the Adelaide Hills Cup  — round two of the Big Blind League’s 2026 season at Simon Tolley Wines in Woodside.

The Big Blind League is a year-long blind tasting competition run as a sport across South Australia’s wine regions, hosted by Bottle Shock founder Brendan Carter.

Sancin is the league’s reigning 2025 grand final champion, back in the field to earn his shot at a title defence. In a competition “where every wine is poured blind and the label counts for nothing”, Sancin began the cup with a score of 16 of 25 after the first round, equal-eleventh in a room with an average of 16.7.

The regional cup went for three rounds. Round one was an options game with five wines, five calls each and a point per correct call. The Hills field was the “strongest yet” with 351 of 525 blind calls correct, making for 67% against 55% at Claire.

The first wine of the Adelaide Hills Cup was a local: a 2024 Adelaide Hills Riesling, poured blind twenty minutes from the vineyard that grew it. Bottle Shock said that only five of the twenty-one tasters on the floor placed it in the Hills. Two pours later, the same room read the host’s own Chardonnay at 89 calls out of a possible 105, the best-read wine of the day.

Round 3 was called ‘The Blackout’ featuring one wine with no colour and no clues.

“Sancin entered as the seven seed and beat the two seed, then the three. Across the bracket, eight seed Harrison Davies knocked out the top-seeded season-record palate in the quarter-finals. The final — seven versus eight, the two players who had to fight their way into the room — was decided over a $168 Burgundy premier cru, invisible in a black glass. Sancin called it better. Siyuan Hua took third, Jordan Kaas fourth,” Bottle Shock explained.

The win put Sancin on top of the season ladder with 131 points and handed him the league’s second ‘Free Run’ — an automatic seat at the grand final on Saturday 5 December where 24 competitors will play for $5,000.

“The reigning champ came back, bombed the easy round, and won the whole thing from the back door. You cannot script that — and in black glasses, nobody can protect a reputation either,” said Bottle Shock founder Brendan Carter.

The next event is the Barossa Bowl on the 19 September, followed by the McLaren Vale Cup on 24 October and the Coonawarra Cup on 14 November.

content:
The South Australian Government will provide $200,000 to the South Australian Wine Industry Association (SAWIA) to deliver a mental health and wellbeing program during 2026-27.

The Wine Industry Wellbeing Program aims to improve access to mental health and wellbeing support for winegrape growers, winemakers, their families, regional businesses and communities “during a period of structural adjustment in the sector”.

Delivered in partnership with SAWIA, the 2026–27 program responds to calls from wine regions at wine industry roundtables, the Riverland Transition and Economic Diversification Think Tank Workshop as well as the Mental Health and Wellbeing Workshop for greater wellbeing support. It recognises the significant challenges facing grape and wine businesses.

“We all know that when people are doing it tough, looking after their mental health and wellbeing is more important than ever,” said Department of Primary Industries and Regions (PIRSA) deputy chief executive Jo Collins.

Collins added that PIRSA understands the significant challenges the wine industry faces and the toll it has taken.

“That’s why we established the National Viticulture and Wine Sector Working Group in 2024 and have continued listening to industry about the support that’s needed. We’ve heard that while existing measures have helped, more support is needed as the industry continues to adapt.

“This funding for the Wine Industry Wellbeing Program will provide practical, ongoing support for wine-growing communities as they navigate change and build a stronger future,” she said.

SAWIA chief executive Inca Lee welcomed the funding, which she said recognises the people behind the economic challenges in the industry.

“South Australian growers and winemakers are facing sustained pressure, and while wellbeing programs are not a substitute for the broader actions needed to improve business viability, they are an important way to support people through this period of adjustment.

“SAWIA is working closely with regional wine associations to ensure support is practical, locally relevant and builds on trusted programs and services already operating in our wine communities. Every region is different, and we want to make sure this funding delivers support where and how it is needed most by growers and winemakers,” Lee said.

The wellbeing program “will deliver locally tailored activities designed to meet the unique needs of each regional wine community”. PIRSA explained that support will be delivered through a series of activities over time, “providing assistance, support and community connection where it is needed most”.

SAWIA said it is working with regional wine organisations across South Australia to deliver and build on existing local wellbeing initiatives. The program will also include Mental Health First Aid training, helping to equip participants with the skills to recognise early signs of distress and connect people with appropriate services.

The announcement comes weeks after Premier Peter Malinauskas hosted a forum “with key representatives from the state’s wine industry to consider a range of solutions to support the sector through this period of transition and help shape a whole-of-government response”.

Devil’s Corner and Tasmania Football Club this week announced a long-term partnership that will see Devil’s Corner become the Official Wine Partner of the Tasmania Devils.

Led by senior winemaker Tom Wallace, Devil’s Corner produces cool climate wines “shaped by the conditions and character of the East Coast”.

Brown Family Wine Group CEO Cameron MacFarlane said the partnership reflected the significance of the Tasmania Devils journey and Devil’s Corner’s belief in what it could mean for the state.

“Having a Tasmanian team competing on the national stage is something people across the state have wanted for generations, and we’re incredibly proud to be part of that journey,” MacFarlane said.

“This is a defining moment for Tasmania. The Devils will give the state a new national platform and create something Tasmanians everywhere can get behind.

“For Devil’s Corner, this is much bigger than putting our name alongside a football club. It’s an opportunity to back an important new chapter for Tasmania and, together, share more of the people, produce, communities and extraordinary places that make this island what it is.”

Tasmania Football Club CEO Brendon Gale said Devil’s Corner was a natural fit for a club being built to represent the whole state.

“We have a rare opportunity to build a football club from the ground up that genuinely reflects Tasmania, who we are, what we value and what we want to become,” Gale said.

“That makes the partners who join us at this stage particularly important. Devil’s Corner brings genuine Tasmanian credentials, an established reputation and an ambition that reaches well beyond the state.

“It’s exactly the kind of partnership we want to build. One grounded in Tasmania, with the ambition to take our story to audiences around Australia.”

Georgia Bruton, chief marketing executive for Brown Family Wine Group, said the partnership was a natural extension of Brown Family Wine Group’s long-standing commitment to Tasmania and its belief in the people and industries shaping the state’s future.

“We’re incredibly proud to be in the Devils’ corner and to stand behind a Club that will fly the flag for Tasmania on the national stage,” Bruton said.

“Our commitment to Tasmania goes well beyond the wines we make here. It’s about investing in the people, places and industries that make this state extraordinary, from wine and tourism to food, hospitality and now football.”

Tasmania Football Club general manager of commercial and partnerships James Creak said Devil’s Corner’s commitment from the Club’s formative years was particularly meaningful.

“The Tasmania Devils are being built to reflect the pride, character and ambition of Tasmania, and we want partners alongside us who genuinely believe in what we’re building,” Creak said.

“Devil’s Corner has been in our corner early. They’re not waiting for the first AFL game or the first major milestone. They’re backing the journey that gets us there.

“That long term commitment gives us an opportunity to build something meaningful together for our members and supporters, and we’re excited about what the partnership can become as the club grows.”

The partnership will extend beyond the football field, with Devil’s Corner and Tasmania Football Club exploring opportunities across member and supporter experiences, events, hospitality, content and special releases.

From match day hospitality to experiences at the Devil’s Corner cellar door on the East Coast, the organisations shared that the ambition is to bring together Tasmania’s sporting culture with its renowned wine, food and tourism offering, “creating memorable experiences for supporters and new ways to discover the state beyond game day”.

The announcement comes as the Tasmania Devils build towards AFL and AFLW entry in 2028.

On Friday 21 August, Wine Communicators of Australia (WCA) announced Peter Bourne as the 2026 NSW ‘Legend of the Vine’ at the 2026 Sydney Royal Wine Awards Lunch.

Known as ‘The Wine Man’, Bourne was described as “an outstanding new addition to the Legend of the Vine, having spent five decades shaping how Australians understand, enjoy and talk about wine”. He has educated thousands through tastings, masterclasses, corporate sessions and public events with “tremendous care and passion”.

“This honour recognises someone of exceptional character; someone held in deep regard by their peers; and someone who has made an outstanding contribution to the Australian wine industry. And, because this award is created by us — Wine Communicators of Australia — the recipient must also embody excellence in how they write, speak, and share the stories of wine,” explained Brian Chase Olson, chair of the WCA NSW chapter committee.

When accepting the award from Chase Olson, Bourne said he was “chuffed and humbled in equal measure”.

“I really like the alignment with the numbers, celebrating 200 years of the Sydney Royal Wine Show and I’ve been in the industry 50 years – exactly one quarter of the time. I turned professional in 1976 when I opened a wine store, and it has been an amazing ride…if you think back 50 years, Chardonnay was so small I needed to beg Murray Tyrrell for 2 or 3 cases of it.

“Chardonnay has had its ups and downs, and now we produce world-class Chardonnay from this country. We are all a bit concerned about the muddle and the puddle we are in, but we’ve been through those cycles before. So now is the time for us to work a little bit harder; our wines have never been better, and we should be really proud of how we’ve moved geographically and climatically and how we’ve adapted grape varieties to suit how we live and the opportunities we have,” Bourne concluded.

WCA said Bourne has built a national profile sharing stories about Australian wineries and the people behind them across multiple platforms: a long-running contributor to Qantas Magazine | Travel Insider, a founding contributor of Gourmet Traveller WINE, a judge and writer for the Australia’s Best Cellar Door Awards and a panel judge for Australia’s Wine List of the Year Awards. He was also named ‘WCA Wine Communicator of the Year’ in 2010.

Bourne’s influence is “especially profound” in New South Wales. Throughout his career, he has championed NSW producers, hosted countless events and helped shape the conversation about the state’s industry. WCA explained he has helped introduce consumers to emerging regions like Orange, Hilltops and Mudgee “long before they were widely recognised” as well as written extensively about NSW’s well-established wine icons, “giving national visibility to the state’s ever-growing wine quality”.

Tiki Wine & Vineyards has become the first vineyard and winery business in New Zealand to achieve regenerative certification status by A Greener World (AGW).

Tiki Wine & Vineyards said the global, independent certification marks a significant milestone for not just the winery, but for the continued development of regenerative viticulture in New Zealand.

The family wine producer explained that regenerative agriculture works with natural systems to improve soil health, increase biodiversity, strengthen water cycles and build greater resilience across the vineyard ecosystem. Certification requires an “independently audited regenerative plan, with progress measured and verified over time”.

For Tiki, this approach is a natural expression of ‘kaitiakitanga’ – the Māori principle of caring for and protecting the land so it can be passed on in better condition to future generations. It is a principle that the winery said has guided the team since its first vines were planted at Waiata Vineyard in North Canterbury.

“This certification is the culmination of many years of commitment from our vineyard and winery teams across numerous growing seasons. We are grateful to the growers, researchers and organisations around the world who openly share their experience and expertise and help others make the transition to regenerative farming,” said Royce McKean, founder and managing director of Tiki Wine & Vineyards.

“We encourage more vineyards to begin their own regenerative journey. Initiatives such as the Regenerative Viticulture Foundation’s One Block Challenge give growers a practical way to trial regenerative practices in a single vineyard block, learn from the results and build from there.

“We believe healthier soils and more resilient vineyards can support both better fruit and wine and a stronger future for winegrowing and the planet,” McKean said.

The winery said the certification will support it in sharing its regenerative journey through its Tiki, Maui and Waiata wine brands in markets around the world.

Wayne Copp, regional executive director at A Greener World, said Tiki Wine & Vineyards “has demonstrated a clear commitment to measurable and continuing improvement across its vineyard operation”.

“We are proud to recognise Tiki as the first vineyard and winery business in New Zealand to achieve Certified Regenerative by AGW status and look forward to supporting the team as its regenerative journey continues,” said Copp.

The winery noted that global interest in regenerative agriculture has continued to grow, with documentaries like Kiss the Ground and Groundswell, narrated by Woody Harrelson and Demi Moore, helping to bring the story of regenerative farming and the ‘One Billion Acres’ movement to a mainstream audience.

Jeremy Gardiner, head of Māori export customers at New Zealand Trade and Enterprise (NZTE), said an increasing global demand for products that reflect consumers’ values has been observed in recent times.

“NZTE helps kiwi businesses understand what matters most to international customers, giving them the insights they need to succeed in competitive export markets. Tiki Wine & Vineyards is a great example of an exporter that has responded to this demand, building a brand that stands out in markets where values-led production is increasingly sought after,” Gardiner said.

The Australian Wine Research Institute (AWRI) has today announced that Dr Mark Krstic will step down as managing director at the end of 2026, following seven years of leadership and a total of 15 years of service to the AWRI.

The AWRI board said it acknowledges Dr Krstic’s significant contribution to the organisation, its people and the wider industry. The board thanked him “for his dedicated leadership of the AWRI and his commitment to stakeholders, partners and the sector”.

“I have loved leading such a talented team of dedicated and passionate professionals who are deeply committed to advancing Australian wine through trusted, world-class science and practical industry solutions,” said Dr Krstic.

“The AWRI is in a strong position, with an exceptional team, deep industry relationships and a clear purpose. I leave the organisation with enormous pride in what has been achieved and with every confidence that the organisation will continue to play a vital role in supporting the future of the Australian grape and wine sector,” he said.

Professor Kiaran Kirk, chair of the AWRI board, said Dr Krstic has led the AWRI with “great distinction” and steered the organisation “through a period of unprecedented challenge and change”.

“On behalf of the board, I want to thank Mark for his leadership, his steadfast commitment, and his tireless advocacy for the sector throughout his time at the AWRI,” said Kirk.

The board will start a search for the AWRI’s next managing director and will work closely with Dr Krstic and the AWRI executive team to enable a smooth leadership transition.

Since becoming managing director in December 2019, the AWRI said Dr Krstic has been a strong advocate for innovation and applied science, with a consistent focus on ensuring research outcomes translate into real-world benefits for the sector. His contribution was recognised in 2020, when he was named ASVO Viticulturist of the Year.

In his position, Dr Krstic successfully launched Affinity Labs, AWRI’s fee-for-service commercial testing lab, and established a CRC-P focused on No and Low (NOLO) alcohol wine production.

The AWRI said he led efforts to secure its core strategic partnership with Wine Australia and Adelaide University, oversaw the successful delivery of the 2022 and 2025 Australian Wine Industry Technical Conferences, and strengthened important ties with international scientific and commercial wine testing laboratories, “keeping Australian wine science at the forefront of global conversations”.

Dr Krstic has also played a longstanding role in smoke taint research and emergency response since 2006. He was central to the AWRI’s response through major bushfire events in 2013, 2019 and 2020, helping growers and producers navigate particularly challenging conditions.

content:
Thousands of tonnes of Marlborough winery waste could be transformed into a valuable resource for vineyards through a new regional programme led by Bragato Research Institute (BRI).

The Marlborough Circular Wine Programme will collect winery lees, the sediment left over from winemaking, and combine it with materials such as compost and biochar to produce a safe, beneficial soil amendment. The initiative aims to reduce waste and emissions while returning organic matter and nutrients to vineyard soils.

BRI explained that large volumes of lees are produced over a relatively short winemaking period during and after vintage.

“They can be expensive to dispose of and place pressure on regional wastewater and waste-management infrastructure. As disposal costs rise and environmental expectations increase, Marlborough wineries need a more sustainable regional alternative,” the organisation said.

Programme leader Dr Seth Laurenson said that the goal is to create a coordinated regional system that safely returns organic matter and its nutrients to vineyard soils.

“This programme is an excellent example of the wine industry, researchers and government working together to solve a costly waste problem and turn it into a regional resource,” said Dr Laurenson.

The programme will “collect lees from participating wineries and process them into a beneficial soil amendment”. Wineries pay a disposal fee “designed to be competitive with landfill costs” and the finished product will be returned to participating vineyards at no additional cost.

Over four years, the programme aims to divert more than 3,500 tonnes of solid lees from landfill and wastewater systems each year, “mitigating around 4,700 tonnes of CO₂-equivalent emissions”.

The four-year programme represents a combined investment of $6.98 million. The government is investing $2.79 million through the Primary Sector Growth Fund, alongside $4.19 million in co-investment from New Zealand Winegrowers and participating wineries. The programme is also supported by The Green Circle and Marlborough District Council.

BRI will lead the scientific testing, quality assurance and system design needed to demonstrate that the model is sustainable and practical at commercial scale. The programme will also develop a business case for establishing a permanent regional facility.

The Marlborough Circular Wine Programme is the first initiative of its kind at commercial scale in New Zealand’s wine sector.

“If we can demonstrate a safe and commercially viable model in Marlborough, the approach could provide a blueprint for other wine regions,” said Dr Laurenson.

On Saturday 22 August, Stefan Sancin took out the Adelaide Hills Cup  — round two of the Big Blind League’s 2026 season at Simon Tolley Wines in Woodside.

The Big Blind League is a year-long blind tasting competition run as a sport across South Australia’s wine regions, hosted by Bottle Shock founder Brendan Carter.

Sancin is the league’s reigning 2025 grand final champion, back in the field to earn his shot at a title defence. In a competition “where every wine is poured blind and the label counts for nothing”, Sancin began the cup with a score of 16 of 25 after the first round, equal-eleventh in a room with an average of 16.7.

The regional cup went for three rounds. Round one was an options game with five wines, five calls each and a point per correct call. The Hills field was the “strongest yet” with 351 of 525 blind calls correct, making for 67% against 55% at Claire.

The first wine of the Adelaide Hills Cup was a local: a 2024 Adelaide Hills Riesling, poured blind twenty minutes from the vineyard that grew it. Bottle Shock said that only five of the twenty-one tasters on the floor placed it in the Hills. Two pours later, the same room read the host’s own Chardonnay at 89 calls out of a possible 105, the best-read wine of the day.

Round 3 was called ‘The Blackout’ featuring one wine with no colour and no clues.

“Sancin entered as the seven seed and beat the two seed, then the three. Across the bracket, eight seed Harrison Davies knocked out the top-seeded season-record palate in the quarter-finals. The final — seven versus eight, the two players who had to fight their way into the room — was decided over a $168 Burgundy premier cru, invisible in a black glass. Sancin called it better. Siyuan Hua took third, Jordan Kaas fourth,” Bottle Shock explained.

The win put Sancin on top of the season ladder with 131 points and handed him the league’s second ‘Free Run’ — an automatic seat at the grand final on Saturday 5 December where 24 competitors will play for $5,000.

“The reigning champ came back, bombed the easy round, and won the whole thing from the back door. You cannot script that — and in black glasses, nobody can protect a reputation either,” said Bottle Shock founder Brendan Carter.

The next event is the Barossa Bowl on the 19 September, followed by the McLaren Vale Cup on 24 October and the Coonawarra Cup on 14 November.

content:
The South Australian Government will provide $200,000 to the South Australian Wine Industry Association (SAWIA) to deliver a mental health and wellbeing program during 2026-27.

The Wine Industry Wellbeing Program aims to improve access to mental health and wellbeing support for winegrape growers, winemakers, their families, regional businesses and communities “during a period of structural adjustment in the sector”.

Delivered in partnership with SAWIA, the 2026–27 program responds to calls from wine regions at wine industry roundtables, the Riverland Transition and Economic Diversification Think Tank Workshop as well as the Mental Health and Wellbeing Workshop for greater wellbeing support. It recognises the significant challenges facing grape and wine businesses.

“We all know that when people are doing it tough, looking after their mental health and wellbeing is more important than ever,” said Department of Primary Industries and Regions (PIRSA) deputy chief executive Jo Collins.

Collins added that PIRSA understands the significant challenges the wine industry faces and the toll it has taken.

“That’s why we established the National Viticulture and Wine Sector Working Group in 2024 and have continued listening to industry about the support that’s needed. We’ve heard that while existing measures have helped, more support is needed as the industry continues to adapt.

“This funding for the Wine Industry Wellbeing Program will provide practical, ongoing support for wine-growing communities as they navigate change and build a stronger future,” she said.

SAWIA chief executive Inca Lee welcomed the funding, which she said recognises the people behind the economic challenges in the industry.

“South Australian growers and winemakers are facing sustained pressure, and while wellbeing programs are not a substitute for the broader actions needed to improve business viability, they are an important way to support people through this period of adjustment.

“SAWIA is working closely with regional wine associations to ensure support is practical, locally relevant and builds on trusted programs and services already operating in our wine communities. Every region is different, and we want to make sure this funding delivers support where and how it is needed most by growers and winemakers,” Lee said.

The wellbeing program “will deliver locally tailored activities designed to meet the unique needs of each regional wine community”. PIRSA explained that support will be delivered through a series of activities over time, “providing assistance, support and community connection where it is needed most”.

SAWIA said it is working with regional wine organisations across South Australia to deliver and build on existing local wellbeing initiatives. The program will also include Mental Health First Aid training, helping to equip participants with the skills to recognise early signs of distress and connect people with appropriate services.

The announcement comes weeks after Premier Peter Malinauskas hosted a forum “with key representatives from the state’s wine industry to consider a range of solutions to support the sector through this period of transition and help shape a whole-of-government response”.

Brown Family Wine Group CEO Cameron MacFarlane said the partnership reflected the significance of the Tasmania Devils journey and Devil’s Corner’s belief in what it could mean for the state.

“Having a Tasmanian team competing on the national stage is something people across the state have wanted for generations, and we’re incredibly proud to be part of that journey,” MacFarlane said.

“This is a defining moment for Tasmania. The Devils will give the state a new national platform and create something Tasmanians everywhere can get behind.

“For Devil’s Corner, this is much bigger than putting our name alongside a football club. It’s an opportunity to back an important new chapter for Tasmania and, together, share more of the people, produce, communities and extraordinary places that make this island what it is.”

Tasmania Football Club CEO Brendon Gale said Devil’s Corner was a natural fit for a club being built to represent the whole state.

“We have a rare opportunity to build a football club from the ground up that genuinely reflects Tasmania, who we are, what we value and what we want to become,” Gale said.

“That makes the partners who join us at this stage particularly important. Devil’s Corner brings genuine Tasmanian credentials, an established reputation and an ambition that reaches well beyond the state.

“It’s exactly the kind of partnership we want to build. One grounded in Tasmania, with the ambition to take our story to audiences around Australia.”

Georgia Bruton, chief marketing executive for Brown Family Wine Group, said the partnership was a natural extension of Brown Family Wine Group’s long-standing commitment to Tasmania and its belief in the people and industries shaping the state’s future.

“We’re incredibly proud to be in the Devils’ corner and to stand behind a Club that will fly the flag for Tasmania on the national stage,” Bruton said.

“Our commitment to Tasmania goes well beyond the wines we make here. It’s about investing in the people, places and industries that make this state extraordinary, from wine and tourism to food, hospitality and now football.”

Tasmania Football Club general manager of commercial and partnerships James Creak said Devil’s Corner’s commitment from the Club’s formative years was particularly meaningful.

“The Tasmania Devils are being built to reflect the pride, character and ambition of Tasmania, and we want partners alongside us who genuinely believe in what we’re building,” Creak said.

“Devil’s Corner has been in our corner early. They’re not waiting for the first AFL game or the first major milestone. They’re backing the journey that gets us there.

“That long term commitment gives us an opportunity to build something meaningful together for our members and supporters, and we’re excited about what the partnership can become as the club grows.”

The partnership will extend beyond the football field, with Devil’s Corner and Tasmania Football Club exploring opportunities across member and supporter experiences, events, hospitality, content and special releases.

From match day hospitality to experiences at the Devil’s Corner cellar door on the East Coast, the organisations shared that the ambition is to bring together Tasmania’s sporting culture with its renowned wine, food and tourism offering, “creating memorable experiences for supporters and new ways to discover the state beyond game day”.

The announcement comes as the Tasmania Devils build towards AFL and AFLW entry in 2028.

WCA said Bourne has built a national profile sharing stories about Australian wineries and the people behind them across multiple platforms: a long-running contributor to Qantas Magazine | Travel Insider, a founding contributor of Gourmet Traveller WINE, a judge and writer for the Australia’s Best Cellar Door Awards and a panel judge for Australia’s Wine List of the Year Awards. He was also named ‘WCA Wine Communicator of the Year’ in 2010.

Bourne’s influence is “especially profound” in New South Wales. Throughout his career, he has championed NSW producers, hosted countless events and helped shape the conversation about the state’s industry. WCA explained he has helped introduce consumers to emerging regions like Orange, Hilltops and Mudgee “long before they were widely recognised” as well as written extensively about NSW’s well-established wine icons, “giving national visibility to the state’s ever-growing wine quality”.

Tiki Wine & Vineyards has become the first vineyard and winery business in New Zealand to achieve regenerative certification status by A Greener World (AGW).

Tiki Wine & Vineyards said the global, independent certification marks a significant milestone for not just the winery, but for the continued development of regenerative viticulture in New Zealand.

The family wine producer explained that regenerative agriculture works with natural systems to improve soil health, increase biodiversity, strengthen water cycles and build greater resilience across the vineyard ecosystem. Certification requires an “independently audited regenerative plan, with progress measured and verified over time”.

For Tiki, this approach is a natural expression of ‘kaitiakitanga’ – the Māori principle of caring for and protecting the land so it can be passed on in better condition to future generations. It is a principle that the winery said has guided the team since its first vines were planted at Waiata Vineyard in North Canterbury.

“This certification is the culmination of many years of commitment from our vineyard and winery teams across numerous growing seasons. We are grateful to the growers, researchers and organisations around the world who openly share their experience and expertise and help others make the transition to regenerative farming,” said Royce McKean, founder and managing director of Tiki Wine & Vineyards.

“We encourage more vineyards to begin their own regenerative journey. Initiatives such as the Regenerative Viticulture Foundation’s One Block Challenge give growers a practical way to trial regenerative practices in a single vineyard block, learn from the results and build from there.

“We believe healthier soils and more resilient vineyards can support both better fruit and wine and a stronger future for winegrowing and the planet,” McKean said.

The winery said the certification will support it in sharing its regenerative journey through its Tiki, Maui and Waiata wine brands in markets around the world.

Wayne Copp, regional executive director at A Greener World, said Tiki Wine & Vineyards “has demonstrated a clear commitment to measurable and continuing improvement across its vineyard operation”.

“We are proud to recognise Tiki as the first vineyard and winery business in New Zealand to achieve Certified Regenerative by AGW status and look forward to supporting the team as its regenerative journey continues,” said Copp.

The winery noted that global interest in regenerative agriculture has continued to grow, with documentaries like Kiss the Ground and Groundswell, narrated by Woody Harrelson and Demi Moore, helping to bring the story of regenerative farming and the ‘One Billion Acres’ movement to a mainstream audience.

Jeremy Gardiner, head of Māori export customers at New Zealand Trade and Enterprise (NZTE), said an increasing global demand for products that reflect consumers’ values has been observed in recent times.

“NZTE helps kiwi businesses understand what matters most to international customers, giving them the insights they need to succeed in competitive export markets. Tiki Wine & Vineyards is a great example of an exporter that has responded to this demand, building a brand that stands out in markets where values-led production is increasingly sought after,” Gardiner said.

The results for the 2026 Yarra Valley Wine Show have been announced following two days of judging at Seville Estate on 11–12 August, with both established names and new trophy winners recognised across the region’s wine industry.

More than 300 entries were assessed across 13 classes, with 13% awarded gold medals, 24% silver medals and 32% bronze medals.

The 2026 show also introduced two new classes, separating Chardonnay and Pinot Noir into Single Vineyard and non-Single Vineyard categories, providing greater recognition of the distinct character and provenance of the region’s wines.

For Kerri Thompson, who took on the role of chair of judges for the first time this year, the quality and breadth of the entries were highlights of the judging.

“What really stood out this year was the overall quality and consistency across the classes. Just as exciting was the diversity of varieties and styles being celebrated. As judges, that diversity makes the process enormously rewarding and gives us a wonderful snapshot of the energy, confidence and creativity within the Yarra Valley right now,” said Thompson.

The trophy winners were celebrated at a presentation evening attended by 120 guests at the Eva and Marc Besen Centre at TarraWarra.

In total, 22 trophies were awarded to 11 different wine producers, with each trophy featuring “a unique piece hand-crafted by local Yarra Valley master potter and sculptor Ted Secombe”.

Coldstream Hills was the “standout trophy winner”, receiving five trophies in total. Its 2025 Coldstream Hills Beenak Chardonnay claimed four major awards: ‘Best Single Vineyard Chardonnay’, ‘Best Chardonnay’, ‘Best White Wine of Show’ and, ultimately, the coveted ‘James Halliday Wine of Show’ trophy. The winery also received the ‘Dr Tony Jordan Best Sparkling Wine’ trophy for its 2018 Coldstream Hills Sparkling.

Hillcrest Vineyard received three trophies for its 2025 Hillcrest Village Pinot Noir, taking out ‘Best Single Vineyard Pinot’, ‘Best Pinot Noir’ and ‘Best Red Wine of Show’.

Yarra Yering was another major trophy recipient, collecting six trophies across four classes. The winery received trophies for ‘Best Other Single White Variety or Blend’, ‘Best Shiraz’, ‘Best Cabernet Blend’ and ‘Best Other Red Blend’, as well as the prestigious ‘Most Successful Exhibitor’ and ‘Most Successful Vineyard’ trophies.

Centare Vineyard received trophies for ‘Best Cabernet Sauvignon’ and was also rewarded as the ‘Best Small Producer’.

Meanwhile, Yeringberg took home the ‘Dr Bailey Carrodus Memorial Perpetual Wine of Provenance Trophy – an award celebrating the consistency and longevity of a wine label across a minimum eight-year span. Yeringberg was recognised for its Cabernet blend represented by the 2015, 2019 and 2024 vintages.

The 2026 presentation evening also recognised “an outstanding contribution to the region’s wine industry”, with Wine Yarra Valley inducting Rob Sutherland, viticulturist and vineyard manager at De Bortoli Wines, into the Yarra Valley Hall of Fame. The induction acknowledges Sutherland’s more than 20-year career and his significant contribution to the local wine industry.

Dr Mark Krstic will step down at the end of 2026. Image supplied

The Australian Wine Research Institute (AWRI) has today announced that Dr Mark Krstic will step down as managing director at the end of 2026, following seven years of leadership and a total of 15 years of service to the AWRI.

The AWRI board said it acknowledges Dr Krstic’s significant contribution to the organisation, its people and the wider industry. The board thanked him “for his dedicated leadership of the AWRI and his commitment to stakeholders, partners and the sector”.

“I have loved leading such a talented team of dedicated and passionate professionals who are deeply committed to advancing Australian wine through trusted, world-class science and practical industry solutions,” said Dr Krstic.

“The AWRI is in a strong position, with an exceptional team, deep industry relationships and a clear purpose. I leave the organisation with enormous pride in what has been achieved and with every confidence that the organisation will continue to play a vital role in supporting the future of the Australian grape and wine sector,” he said.

Professor Kiaran Kirk, chair of the AWRI board, said Dr Krstic has led the AWRI with “great distinction” and steered the organisation “through a period of unprecedented challenge and change”.

“On behalf of the board, I want to thank Mark for his leadership, his steadfast commitment, and his tireless advocacy for the sector throughout his time at the AWRI,” said Kirk.

The board will start a search for the AWRI’s next managing director and will work closely with Dr Krstic and the AWRI executive team to enable a smooth leadership transition.

Since becoming managing director in December 2019, the AWRI said Dr Krstic has been a strong advocate for innovation and applied science, with a consistent focus on ensuring research outcomes translate into real-world benefits for the sector. His contribution was recognised in 2020, when he was named ASVO Viticulturist of the Year.

In his position, Dr Krstic successfully launched Affinity Labs, AWRI’s fee-for-service commercial testing lab, and established a CRC-P focused on No and Low (NOLO) alcohol wine production.

The AWRI said he led efforts to secure its core strategic partnership with Wine Australia and Adelaide University, oversaw the successful delivery of the 2022 and 2025 Australian Wine Industry Technical Conferences, and strengthened important ties with international scientific and commercial wine testing laboratories, “keeping Australian wine science at the forefront of global conversations”.

Dr Krstic has also played a longstanding role in smoke taint research and emergency response since 2006. He was central to the AWRI’s response through major bushfire events in 2013, 2019 and 2020, helping growers and producers navigate particularly challenging conditions.
